extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, basic properties, and canonical examples of metrics, pseudometrics, inner products, norms, open sets, and related lemmas in the context of analysis; suitable for learning or teaching a first course in metric-space theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a metric
rubrics_metrics.description: A function d from X×X to the real numbers is a metric (distance function) if (i) d(x,y) ≥ 0 with equality iff x = y, (ii) d(x,y)=d(y,x) for all x,y in X, (iii) d(x,z) ≤ d(x,y)+d(y,z) (triangle inequality). In this case the pair (X,d) is called a metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the canonical requirement to produce a metric space. Many subsequent constructions are shown to satisfy these three properties; failure of (i) (identity of indiscernibles) is the main reason some constructions yield only a pseudometric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a pseudometric
rubrics_metrics.description: Weakened version of (i): (i0) d(x,y) ≥ 0 and d(x,x)=0 always (but d(x,y)=0 need not imply x=y). If (i0), (ii), and (iii) hold then d is a pseudometric and (X,d) is a pseudometric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to classify examples where distinct points may have distance zero (e.g. L1 or L2 distances on integrable functions that differ on a set of measure zero or at a point). Authors explicitly point out when a construction yields only a pseudometric rather than a true metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open ball (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For (X,d) a pseudometric space and r>0, the open ball centered at x of radius r is B(r,x) = { y in X | d(x,y) < r }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Open balls are the basic neighborhoods used to define open sets and continuity in metric spaces; many proofs revolve around containment and triangle-inequality manipulations of balls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open set (metric definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset U of X is open if for each x in U there exists r>0 such that the open ball B(r,x) is contained in U. For the line this reproduces the usual notion of open intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent characterization: open sets are arbitrary unions of open balls (Lemma 2.1). This is the operative definition for topological concepts derived from a metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open ball is open; open sets are unions of balls (Lemma 2.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: In any pseudometric space every open ball is an open set. The open sets are exactly all possible unions of open balls.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides the tool used repeatedly to show openness: show a set is union of balls. Proof uses triangle inequality to find a ball around each point contained in a given ball.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection-of-balls lemma (Lemma 2.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: If z is in the intersection of two open balls B(r,x) and B(s,y), then there exists t>0 such that the open ball B(t,z) is contained in the intersection. Consequently the intersection of two open balls is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful device in proofs that finite intersections of open sets are open; gives an explicit t in terms of r,s and distances to z.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic algebra of open sets (Proposition 2.5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Open sets satisfy: (a) X and ∅ are open; (b) arbitrary unions of open sets are open; (c) finite intersections of open sets are open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard closure properties of the metric-topology; (c) is proved by reducing to the intersection of two open sets then using Lemma 2.4.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner product (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inner product (real case) or Hermitian inner product (complex case) on a vector space V is a form (·,·) : V×V → R (or C) satisfying: (i) linearity in the first variable, (ii) conjugate linearity in the second variable (complex case), (iii) symmetry / Hermitian symmetry ( (y,x) = overline{(x,y)} ), (iv) definiteness: (x,x) > 0 for x ≠ 0. The pair (V,(·,·)) is an inner-product space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The inner product axioms are the starting point for defining a norm by ||x|| = (x,x)^{1/2} and for developing orthogonality, Schwarz inequality, and the induced metric. The text also explains the complex vs real differences and the naming 'Hermitian' for the complex case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo inner-product and pseudonorm (semidefinite case)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (·,·) satisfies (i)–(iii) but is only semidefinite so (x,x) ≥ 0 with (x,x)=0 possible for nonzero x, the pair is a pseudo inner-product space and kxk = (x,x)^{1/2} is a pseudonorm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many function-space examples (e.g. L1, L2 on integrable functions) give only a pseudo inner-product because distinct functions can have zero 'norm' (e.g., differ on null sets or single points). The Schwarz inequality and triangle inequality are still valid but proofs may need extra handling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schwarz inequality in (pseudo) inner-product spaces (Lemma 2.2)
rubrics_metrics.description: For V a pseudo inner-product space and x,y in V, |(x,y)| ≤ ||x|| ||y||.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statement and short proof handling the semidefinite complication; this inequality is used to deduce the triangle inequality for norms and to justify Euclidean-norm triangle behavior in R^n and C^n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangle inequality for the norm and induced pseudometric (Proposition 2.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: If V is a pseudo inner-product space then the pseudonorm satisfies ||x+y|| ≤ ||x|| + ||y||, scalar multiplication property, and ||cx|| = |c| ||x||. The formula d(x,y) = ||x-y|| defines a pseudometric; when the form is definite this is a metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how inner-product structures produce (pseudo)metric spaces; standard routine using Schwarz inequality and bilinearity. Emphasizes when the induced distance is only a pseudometric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Euclidean space R^n metric and Euclidean norm (Example 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rn with the Euclidean norm ||x|| = (Σ x_j^2)^{1/2} and d(x,y)=||x-y|| is a metric space. Properties: (a) ||cx|| = |c| ||x||, (b) ||x|| ≥ 0 with equality iff x=0, (c) triangle inequality derived via dot product and Schwarz inequality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serves as the motivating example; the dot product is the inner product used to establish (c). Notes about geometric interpretation of open balls for n=1,2,3 and equivalence with standard multivariable calculus open sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex Euclidean space C^n via Hermitian inner product (Example 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cn becomes a metric space using the Hermitian inner product (z,w) = Σ z_j overline{w_j}, norm ||z||=(z,z)^{1/2}, and d(z,w)=||z-w||. Alternatively identify Cn with R^{2n} and use the real Euclidean metric; both give the same metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains two equivalent constructions and mentions the Hermitian inner product generalizes the dot product; used to justify Schwarz inequality and triangle inequality in complex vector spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extended real line metric R* (Example 3)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a bijection f from (-1,1) onto R, extend to include endpoints mapping to ±∞, and define d(x,x') = |f(x) - f(x')|. With monotonicity of f this gives a metric on R* whose open balls are intervals (a,b] etc., and intersections with R produce ordinary open sets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates constructing a metric on a compactified/extended real line by monotone transform; proof of triangle inequality uses monotonicity and splitting into three cases for relative order of points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniform metric on bounded functions (sup metric) (Example 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S a nonempty set let B(S) be bounded scalar-valued functions on S. Define d(f,g) = sup_{s in S} |f(s)-g(s)|. Then (B(S),d) is a metric space (convergence in d is uniform convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key standard metric for spaces of bounded functions; used to relate metric convergence to uniform convergence. Authors note scalars may be R or C and generalization follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generalization: bounded functions into any metric space (Example 5)
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace the range by any metric space (R,ρ). Fix r0 in R and consider bounded functions f:S→R (bounded meaning sup_s ρ(f(s),r0) < ∞). Define d(f,g)=sup_s ρ(f(s),g(s)) to get a metric space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows the sup construction works when targets are arbitrary metric spaces; independence of choice of r0 argued using triangle inequality in the range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequence space ℓ^2 metric (Example 6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Space of scalar sequences {c_n} with Σ |c_n|^2 < ∞. Define d(c,d) = (Σ |c_n - d_n|^2)^{1/2}. This metric is natural for Fourier-coefficient sequences; triangle inequality follows by standard ℓ^2 arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies ℓ^2 as a canonical Hilbert-space example; emphasizes relation to Fourier coefficients of square-integrable functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indiscrete pseudometric (Example 7)
rubrics_metrics.description: If d(x,y)=0 for all x,y in a nonempty set X then d is a pseudometric and the only open sets are X and ∅ (if X has >1 element d is not a metric).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives an extreme example of a pseudometric with trivial topology; useful as a counterexample where identity of indiscernibles fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrete metric (Example 8)
rubrics_metrics.description: d(x,y)=0 if x=y, and d(x,y)=1 if x≠y. Then d is a metric and every subset of X is open.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canonical example giving the discrete topology; used to contrast with indiscrete example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hamming-type metric on S^n (component-difference count) (Example 9)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S nonempty and integer n>0, define d(x,y) = number of components where x_j ≠ y_j for n-tuples x,y in S^n. This d is a metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a finite combinatorial metric; every subset is open (like discrete metric). Proof of triangle inequality is left as an exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hedgehog space (Example 10)
rubrics_metrics.description: On R^2, single out origin 0. Define ρ(x,y)=d(x,y) (Euclidean) + d(x,0) if x and y are on same ray from 0; otherwise ρ(x,y)=d(x,0)+d(0,y). Then ρ is a metric; some sets are open in (X,ρ) but not in Euclidean metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibits a nonstandard metric on the plane that changes local structure near the origin; useful for examples where metrics induce strictly different topologies even on the same underlying set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert cube metric (Example 11)
rubrics_metrics.description: X = sequences {x_m} with 0 ≤ x_m ≤ 1 and metric d(x,y)=Σ 2^{-m} |x_m - y_m|. This defines a metric on the set (the triangle inequality established by termwise estimates and letting N→∞).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard compact metric-space example (Hilbert cube). The weights 2^{-m} ensure convergence of the series and compatibility with product topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: L1 metric on Riemann integrable functions (Example 12)
rubrics_metrics.description: For [a,b] a bounded interval and X the Riemann integrable complex-valued functions on [a,b], define d1(f,g) = ∫_a^b |f(x)-g(x)| dx. Then (X,d1) is a pseudometric: possible that d1(f,g)=0 without f=g (e.g., differ at a single point).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains why L1 on Riemann integrable functions yields only a pseudometric (pointwise differences can have zero integral). Contrast with equivalence-class construction used in Lebesgue/Lp theory to get a true metric on equivalence classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: L2 metric on periodic Riemann-integrable functions (Example 13)
rubrics_metrics.description: For 2π-periodic Riemann integrable functions on [-π,π], define d2(f,g) = (1/(2π) ∫_{-π}^{π} |f(x)-g(x)|^2 dx)^{1/2}. Then (X,d2) is a pseudometric (distinct functions can have zero distance); triangle inequality required special Lemma 1.62 to handle zero-norm cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the L^2-style pseudometric used in Fourier-series context. The text notes the need for a careful argument (via earlier lemmas) to handle functions with zero norm and to prove the Schwarz/triangle inequalities in this setting.
